title: Clean Architecture for Web APIs (layers and dependency rule)
hook: A Web API that puts SQL queries inside controllers becomes impossible to test and painful to change. Clean Architecture organizes code into layers — Domain, Application, Infrastructure, Presentation — with a strict dependency rule: inner layers never reference outer layers.

blocks.text: Clean Architecture (popularized by Robert C. Martin) separates business rules from frameworks and databases. For ASP.NET Core Web APIs: Domain holds entities and value objects with zero framework references. Application holds use cases (commands/queries), interfaces for repositories and messaging, and DTOs. Infrastructure implements EF Core DbContext, SQS publishers, email senders. Presentation is controllers or minimal API endpoints that call Application services. Dependencies point inward — Infrastructure references Application, never the reverse.

entries.plainDefinition: Source code dependencies only point inward — Domain has no outward dependencies.
entries.example: Application defines IOrderRepository; Infrastructure implements it

entries.plainDefinition: Entities, value objects, domain events, business invariants — pure C#.
entries.example: public class Order { public void Ship() { ... } }

entries.plainDefinition: Use cases orchestrating domain logic; defines ports (interfaces) for infrastructure.
EF Core, SQS, external HTTP clients — framework and IO implementations.

blocks.text: Senior interviews at product companies ask how you structure a microservice for testability and team scaling. Clean Architecture lets you unit test PlaceOrderHandler with a fake IOrderRepository without spinning up a database. It prevents EF Core entities leaking into every layer. The tradeoff is more projects and interfaces — overkill for a prototype, essential for long-lived APIs with multiple developers.

blocks.title: Pragmatic Clean Architecture
blocks.body: You do not need 10 projects on day one. Start with Domain + Application + Infrastructure + Api folders in one solution. Add MediatR for command/query dispatch. Extract projects when boundaries stabilize.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: HTTP request hits Presentation
items.body: Controller or minimal API endpoint receives POST /orders.

items.title: Dispatch to Application
items.body: Endpoint sends PlaceOrderCommand via MediatR to PlaceOrderHandler.

items.title: Domain logic executes
items.body: Handler loads Order via IOrderRepository, calls domain methods, enforces invariants.

items.title: Infrastructure persists
items.body: EfOrderRepository saves via DbContext; OutboxMessage written in same transaction.

items.title: Response returns
items.body: Handler returns OrderDto mapped from domain entity — no EF entity in HTTP response.

snippet.label: Domain entity with business logic
snippet.explanation: Domain encapsulates invariants. No data annotations, no EF attributes — pure business rules testable without any framework.

snippet.label: Application handler and port interface
snippet.explanation: Application defines the port (IOrderRepository) and use case (handler). Depends on Domain only. Infrastructure will implement IOrderRepository.

snippet.label: Infrastructure EF implementation and API endpoint
snippet.explanation: Infrastructure implements port with EF. API is thin — dispatches command, returns result. DI registration in Presentation/Infrastructure project.

snippet.label: Unit test Application without database
snippet.explanation: Application layer unit tests use fake repositories — fast, no WebApplicationFactory needed. Integration tests still verify EF wiring separately.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Anemic domain model — entities are DTO bags, all logic in handlers. EF entities used as domain entities — persistence concerns leak into Domain. Application referencing Infrastructure — breaks dependency rule. Over-abstracting with IRepository<T> for every entity when DbContext suffices. Clean Architecture ceremony on a 3-endpoint CRUD API.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: Application project has zero PackageReference to Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore — enforce with architecture tests (NetArchTest.Rules). Code review rejects DbContext in controllers. Team ownership: Domain+Application owned by feature team, Infrastructure shared platform team. MediatR pipeline behaviors for logging, validation, transactions wrap handlers consistently. When to bend the rule: read-heavy reporting endpoints may query DbContext directly in Infrastructure query services — document the exception.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Cannot explain the dependency rule or draw layer diagram. Saying Clean Architecture means 'use a repository for everything'. Application layer referencing EF Core types. Unable to contrast with vertical slice or when to skip layers for a small API.

interviewTakeaways: Dependency rule: dependencies point inward — Domain has zero framework references.
Application defines ports (interfaces); Infrastructure implements them — enables unit testing handlers with fakes.
Production tip: NetArchTest enforces layer rules in CI; MediatR behaviors for cross-cutting concerns.

60s: Domain entities with business logic. Application handlers + IOrderRepository interface. Infrastructure EF implementation. Thin API dispatches MediatR command. Dependencies: Infra → App → Domain only.
Follow-up: Clean Architecture vs vertical slice — when would you choose each?
commonPitfalls: Cannot state dependency rule gets you rejected — inner layers never depend on outer layers.
IRepository<T> for everything without justification — over-abstraction red flag.

Strong answer: 'Domain pure C#. Application use cases + ports. Infrastructure EF/SQS. API thin. Test handlers with fake repo. NetArchTest in CI. Vertical slices for smaller teams. Repository only when swapping persistence.'
introducedIn: Pattern by Robert C. Martin; common in .NET since ~2018 with MediatR adoption

jsTsCorrelations.note: NestJS modules enforce boundaries: DomainModule exports entities, ApplicationModule imports Domain, InfrastructureModule provides TypeORM repositories implementing application ports — same dependency inversion.

Express apps often use routes → services → repositories folder structure — informal Clean Architecture. Missing enforcement means routes import pg directly — equivalent to DbContext in controllers anti-pattern.
